transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well, I'm here because for months now, I’ve been trying to get people to understand what's happening. My husband’s family is... they're quietly messing with our money and our good name. 

It shows up in these little ways. Like, I'll see little billing errors show up at my work, or someone at church will suddenly act funny toward me out of nowhere. And no matter what records anyone pulls up to try and explain it away, I know it ties back to them. I just need someone to actually hear me on this.

When you notice these things happening — like the billing errors or people acting strangely toward you — do you ever see, hear, or perceive anything unusual that others around you don't seem to notice?

No, I don't hear voices or see things, if that's what you're asking. I'm not imagining things. 

The billing errors I catch at work are right there on the screen or the paper. Anyone can look at them. And the way people act at church, that's just how they're actually behaving in the moment. It's not that I'm seeing or hearing things that aren't there... it's just that other people don't realize why these things are happening, or who is actually behind it. So, no, nothing like that.

If your husband or a trusted friend showed you clear evidence that his family wasn't involved in these things — like bank records or explanations for the billing errors — would you be able to consider that possibility, or do you feel certain that no amount of evidence could change your mind about what's really going on?

Well, like I was saying before... it really doesn't matter what records anyone pulls up. My husband has actually tried doing exactly that. He's shown me bank statements, and people at my job try to explain away the billing errors as just normal mistakes or computer glitches. 

But I know it ties back to his family. They are the ones quietly messing with our money and our good name. So... no, looking at more records or explanations wouldn't change my mind, because I know what's really going on. I've been trying to get people to understand this for months now. The paperwork might look fine to everyone else, but I know they're the ones behind it.

Besides what's happening with your husband's family and the money, have you noticed other people or groups working against you in other areas of your life — like at work, in your neighborhood, or anywhere else?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean... it's really just his family. 

I don't have any issues with my neighbors, and my coworkers are fine. Like I said about the billing errors at my job, I know it's his family behind them, not the people I actually work with. I don't think there's anyone else involved. So, no, it's not like the whole world is out to get me or anything like that. It is specifically them.

You mentioned that looking at bank statements and explanations from your coworkers wouldn't change your mind. But let me ask this differently: is there anything — any kind of evidence or explanation — that could possibly make you reconsider whether his family might not be involved in these things?

No, there isn't. I mean, I'm here because for months now I've been trying to get people to understand exactly what's going on. My husband's family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. 

It's just obvious to me. Like when those little billing errors show up at work, or when someone at church suddenly acts funny toward me... I know it ties back to them. No matter what records anyone pulls up or what kind of explanation they try to give me, I just know they're behind it. So, no, there isn't any evidence that would make me reconsider, because I already know the truth.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a circumscribed, non-bizarre delusional belief system centered on husband's family deliberately sabotaging finances and reputation through subtle means (billing errors, social manipulation). The belief is held with absolute conviction despite contrary evidence (bank statements, explanations from coworkers and husband). No hallucinations, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms are present. Functional impairment is evident (months of distress, seeking validation). The delusion is isolated to this specific theme without expansion to other persecutors or domains, consistent with delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia or brief psychotic disorder.
